title: Astronauts float because they’re falling, not because gravity is gone
body: Gravity doesn’t switch off in orbit: at the height of the International Space Station it is still about **90%** as strong as on the ground. Astronauts feel weightless because they and the station are falling together, all the time, so nothing pushes back on them. The station also moves sideways at about 7.7 km per second, so fast that as it falls, Earth’s curved surface keeps dropping away beneath it. Isaac Newton described the idea with an imaginary cannon on a mountain.

slides.question: At the height of the ISS, how strong is gravity compared with on the ground?
slides.explanation: Roughly 90%. Height alone barely weakens gravity. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling together, moving sideways so fast that Earth keeps curving away beneath them.

slides.alt: A copperplate-style engraving: a cannon on a mountain fires balls ever faster, each landing farther around the Earth, until one circles the planet. It becomes a modern diagram of the ISS orbiting 400 km up, where gravity is still about 90%, with a crew falling along with the station.
slides.music: “Cello Suite #1 in G - Prelude” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.heading: Newton’s cannon
slides.text: In an early draft of his *Principia*, published in 1728, Isaac Newton imagined firing a stone from a high mountain with no air in the way. Too slow, and it falls back to Earth. At just the right speed, it circles the planet and comes back to the mountain. [More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newton%27s_cannonball)

left.label: Myth
left.text: There’s no gravity in space, so astronauts drift around.

right.label: Fact
right.text: Gravity keeps the ISS in orbit. Crew and station fall together, so nothing presses on the crew.

slides.heading: Faster still
slides.text: Fire faster than the speed that makes a circle, and the path stretches into an ellipse. At escape velocity or above, the ball never comes back at all.

slides.heading: Match the ISS numbers
slides.explanation: At 7.7 km/s the station laps Earth every 93 minutes, about 15.5 times a day, so the crew sees roughly 16 sunrises.

slides.heading: 16 sunrises a day
slides.text: One lap takes about 93 minutes, or around 15.5 orbits a day, so the crew sees about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every 24 hours. They cover the windows when it is time to sleep.
